world_behind.title: A law protecting a minority faith
world_behind.text: The church complains of persecution; Alma takes it to the king; Mosiah issues a proclamation forbidding any unbeliever to persecute a church member. The state does not endorse the church. It makes harassing it illegal, a narrower thing, and the record treats it as sufficient.

world_behind.title: The church legislates its own equality
world_behind.text: Alongside the royal proclamation runs a strict command inside the churches: no persecutions among them, an equality among all men, no pride or haughtiness, every man esteeming his neighbor as himself, and the priests working for their own living. The rules Alma the elder made at the waters of Mormon are now the law of a national church.

world_behind.title: Two founders' sons, on the wrong side
world_behind.text: The sons of Mosiah and a son of Alma are named among the unbelievers. The king's heirs and the high priest's namesake are together in a campaign to destroy the church, and the record puts them in the same clause.

world_behind.title: A conversion in borrowed wording
world_behind.text: He falls to the earth; a voice asks why he persecutes; he is struck helpless and has to be carried; he is blind to what was said until he recovers. The wording of the angel's question is the wording of the voice on the Damascus road, which the New Testament tells three times.

world_behind.title: A father praying for a son, and being told so
world_behind.text: The angel says he has come because Alma the elder prayed with much faith, and that the purpose is that those prayers might be answered. The record makes the intervention a response to a specific petition.

world_behind.title: A kingdom with no heir, as of this chapter
world_behind.text: All four of Mosiah's sons are named here, and all four are among the unbelievers before the angel comes. By the end of the chapter they are travelling preachers. The succession problem that occupies Mosiah 29 is created in verse 8 and sealed in verse 34, and the record does not point at it.

words.text: Arrogance carried in bearing rather than in speech, the visible form of pride. The command pairs it with pride and makes both a threat to peace. What the verse asks for instead is that every man esteem his neighbor as himself.

An obstruction, something that slows a thing down. It occurs once in scripture, and the record applies it to a young man's whole campaign against the church. The word names a drag on prosperity. The verbs around it are stealing away hearts and causing dissension.

Being stunned, knocked out of one's senses. It appears three times in seven verses and it is the chapter's physical mechanism: they fall, they fall again, and finally Alma cannot speak or move. Nothing is said about fear; the record keeps naming the shock instead.

Recounted in order, went back over. The men who had been helping him attack the church are the ones who tell his father what happened, and the word implies a full and sequential account. The father's response is to gather a crowd.

Moving through something that resists: water, mud, depth. Alma uses it of tribulation, which turns the suffering into a medium rather than an event. The clause that follows is "repenting nigh unto death."

A depth without a bottom. Alma calls it the darkest one, and sets it directly against the marvelous light in the next clause. The pairing is spatial rather than moral: he describes where he was and where he now is, and lets the reader supply the judgment.

phrases.term: Every man should esteem his neighbor as himself
phrases.text: The church's internal rule, and it occurs once in scripture. Alma the elder had taught his people at Helam to love their neighbor as themselves, and had refused a crown on the ground that no one should esteem one flesh above another. Both sentences turn up here as enacted policy.

phrases.term: He was a man of many words, and did speak much flattery
phrases.text: The charge against Alma the younger, in the vocabulary this record reserves for Noah's priests. Flattering words had deceived a people into idolatry in chapter 11 and drawn church members into sin in chapter 26. Here the same instrument is in the hands of a high priest's son.

phrases.term: Why persecutest thou the church of God?
phrases.text: The angel's question, and it is the question asked on the Damascus road with one substitution: there the voice said "me," here it says "the church of God." The verse before has him falling to the earth, which is also how that account opens.

phrases.term: Remember the captivity of thy fathers in the land of Helam
phrases.text: The angel's instruction is to remember somebody else's history. Alma the younger was not in Helam; his father was, and had his burdens made light there. The argument put to him is not about his own experience at all.

phrases.term: He became dumb, that he could not open his mouth
phrases.text: A man of many words losing the use of them. He also cannot move his hands and has to be carried, which the verse calls being carried helpless. Everything the chapter said he was good at is taken away at once.

phrases.term: The Lord in mercy hath seen fit to snatch me out of an everlasting burning
phrases.text: Isaiah has an everlasting burning that nobody can dwell with. The sentence puts the phrase in the first person and adds the rescue, and the words "seen fit" are the same construction the record used of the Lord's decisions about two peoples in bondage.

phrases.term: Redeemed from the gall of bitterness and bonds of iniquity
phrases.text: Peter said almost this to a man in Samaria who tried to buy the Spirit. The second half is also his own father's phrase: Alma the elder had told the people at Helam that they had been bound with the bands of iniquity and delivered from them. The son describes his rescue in his father's words.

phrases.term: They did publish peace; they did publish good tidings of good
phrases.text: Isaiah's line about the runner with beautiful feet, applied to the sons of Mosiah. Abinadi had expounded that verse in Noah's court and given the feet finally to the Lord himself. Here the record hands the description to four young men who had been trying to destroy the church.

verses.label: v. 1–5
verses.title: A law, and a rule
verses.text: The church complains, the king proclaims that unbelievers may not persecute, and the churches issue their own strict command: equality, no pride, esteem your neighbor as yourself, and priests supporting themselves by their own labor. The state protects; the church regulates itself.

verses.label: v. 6–9
verses.title: Prosperity, and one young man
verses.text: The people scatter, build cities in all quarters, and grow wealthy. Then the record names the sons of Mosiah among the unbelievers and one of Alma's sons among them, and describes what he does with words: flattery, stolen hearts, dissension.

verses.label: v. 10–13
verses.title: An interruption
verses.text: They are going about secretly to destroy the church when an angel descends in a cloud with a voice like thunder that shakes the ground. They fall and do not understand him. He cries again, and the second time it is a question with a name attached.

verses.label: v. 14–17
verses.title: Why the angel came
verses.text: Not for Alma's sake, according to the angel: the Lord heard the prayers of his people and of Alma's father, who had prayed with much faith. The stated purpose is that those prayers be answered. Then comes the instruction to remember the captivity of thy fathers, and he departs.

verses.label: v. 18–23
verses.title: Carried in, prayed over
verses.text: They fall a second time, and Alma cannot speak or move. He is carried to his father, who rejoices and gathers a crowd and the priests. Two days and two nights of fasting later his limbs receive their strength and he stands up and tells them to be of good comfort.

verses.label: v. 24–31
verses.title: What he says when he can speak
verses.text: Born of the Spirit; all mankind must be born again, changed from a carnal and fallen state to a state of righteousness; they become new creatures. Then his own case in violent terms: wading, snatched, the darkest abyss, the marvelous light. The section closes with a scene where every knee bows.

verses.label: v. 32–37
verses.title: The rest of their lives, in six verses
verses.text: They travel, publish what they have seen, are persecuted and smitten, confirm the church, and work to repair the injuries they had done. Four of them are named as the sons of Mosiah. The last verse gives them Isaiah's beautiful feet.

chapter.title: One word separates this question from Saul's
chapter.text: "Why persecutest thou the church of God?" against "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" In both accounts the man has just fallen to the earth. The New Testament tells that story three times; this record tells this one three times as well, here and twice more in Alma's own voice.

chapter.title: The intervention is credited to somebody else's prayers
chapter.text: The angel says twice that he has come so that the prayers of Alma's father and of the church might be answered. Nothing in the passage is presented as being about the young man's readiness or merit, and verse 16 goes further: seek to destroy the church no more, even if thou wilt of thyself be cast off.

chapter.title: What is taken from him is exactly what he was good at
chapter.text: Verse 8 calls him a man of many words. Verse 19 has him unable to open his mouth, unable to move his hands, and carried. The record does not comment on the fit.

chapter.title: He is told to remember a history he was not present for
chapter.text: The captivity in Helam and in Nephi belonged to his father's generation. The angel treats an inherited deliverance as a claim on him, which is the same appeal Benjamin and Limhi both made to their own peoples.

chapter.title: The record makes his conversion the source of a vocabulary
chapter.text: Darkest abyss, marvelous light, racked with eternal torment, wading through much tribulation. Alma will reach for these again when he tells the story to Helaman, and Ammon will use two of them in a sermon of his own. What is coined here is reused for the rest of the book.

chapter.title: Two days and two nights, and the phrase has one other home
chapter.text: Alma lies helpless for that span while the priests fast. Years later a Lamanite king lies as though dead for the same span, and Ammon (one of the men carrying Alma here) is standing in the room for that one too. The record uses the phrase four times, and three of them belong to the later episode.

chapter.title: The chapter ends by handing Isaiah's runner to the persecutors
chapter.text: Publish peace, publish good tidings of good, declare that the Lord reigneth. Abinadi had expounded that passage to the court that killed him. Four men who had set out to destroy the church end the chapter described in its words.

chapter.title: Role in the book
chapter.text: Mosiah 26 gave the church a rule for transgressors; this chapter gives it the hardest possible test case and answers it with an angel. What follows is immediate: the sons of Mosiah ask to go to the Lamanites, and the kingdom has no heir.

applications.title: Protect without endorsing
applications.text: Mosiah did not make the church official; he made persecuting it illegal. Where you have authority over a disagreement, forbidding the harm is often the whole of what is yours to do.

applications.title: Keep praying for the person who is not listening
applications.text: The angel came so that a father's prayers might be answered. Nothing in the account suggests the son was moving toward it, and the record credits the outcome to the praying rather than to the timing.

applications.title: Notice what your gift is being used for
applications.text: He was a man of many words and used them for flattery and dissension. The same capacity that made him effective made him dangerous, and the record names it as the instrument rather than the excuse.

applications.title: Ask what a deliverance you did not live through has to do with you
applications.text: The angel told him to remember his fathers' captivity. Inherited rescues make a claim; the question is whether you have ever worked out what it is.

applications.title: Say the hard version out loud
applications.text: Wading through tribulation, repenting nigh unto death, the darkest abyss. He did not soften his own account when he finally had a voice, and the specificity is what makes it useful to anybody else.

applications.title: Repair what you can reach
applications.text: They traveled the whole land zealously striving to repair the injuries they had done, confessing their sins. Restitution here is described as effort and travel.

applications.title: Let somebody carry you
applications.text: He could not speak or move and had to be brought to his father by the men who had been helping him do wrong. Being carried is not a failure state; it is how he got where he needed to be.

questions.text: What am I good at that I am currently using badly?
What have I opposed that I have never let anyone ask me about directly?
Whose prayers am I the subject of?
Which of my family's hard histories have I never actually reckoned with?
What would I say if I had two days of silence and then a voice?
What injury of mine is still within reach of repair?
